practice_span: I have painted on walls since I was ten. It has been twenty-six years.
craft_description: I say this is our story on the wall, in rice white. To children I say, every person in it is doing some work.
craft_distinct: With just circles, triangles and lines we paint our whole life.
motif_meaning: The Tarpa dance circle. It means being together and joy. White on red earth feels true.
motif_story: I painted the Tarpa on a school wall. The children saw it and began dancing in a circle, holding hands.
colour_change: Earlier only earth and rice white. Now we also use acrylic on paper. The lines stayed the same.
specialisation: A line that moves without stopping. I began attaching a story card to each painting.
known_for: The village women call me to draw the wedding chowk.
craft_keep_change: I would keep the rice white. I would change the price set by the middleman.
local_belonging_phrase: “Our painting belongs on our wall. Forest, field, dance, all of it is from here.”
place_belonging_feeling: Dahanu's forest, fields and festivals made these paintings. That is my pride.
ecological_input: We coat the wall with cow dung and red earth. The rice is from our own field, ground to make the white. We chew a bamboo stick to make a brush.
place_use_moment: Before Diwali I coated the wall with dung and painted a harvest scene on it.
place_missing: Without a dung wall I must use paper or canvas, but the link to the home breaks.
place_change: Now concrete houses have come, and dung walls are fewer. Talk of the highway and the port has raised fear about our land, and the forest has shrunk too.
place_before_after: Earlier every house wall had paintings; now there are concrete houses and paintings on paper.
emotion_about_place_change: “If the wall goes, the painting will move to paper. But if the land goes, what will we paint?”
teacher_name_relation: My grandmother, Sakhubai. She drew the wedding chowk in the village as a suvasini.
teaching_memory: My grandmother sat me in front of the wall. I drew a person, and she said, “What is their work?” I drew again and put a plough in the hand. Then she laughed.
remembered_phrase_gesture: “First the circle, then the work.” Saying this, she would turn the stick in a circle in the air.
family_generations: My grandmother and mother painted. My sister and I paint. My daughter Priya is in school and paints in the holidays. My brother now paints on paper too.
family_line: Grandmother Sakhubai → mother → my sister and me → daughter Priya.
transmission_strength:
Children quickly learn the Tarpa dance and field scenes, because they see them every day.

The rules of the wedding chowk and the songs that go with it. Few suvasinis who know them are left.
teaching_practice: In the Saturday class I first teach drawing the circle, then giving each person work.
teaching_scene: We sat on the school veranda. I slowly turned the stick in the girl's hand in a circle.
teaching_difficulty: Children's schooling and going to the city for work. Also, they want to learn only what sells fast.
primary_material:
Rice flour, cow dung, red earth, a bamboo stick. Canvas or paper for selling.

Rice, earth and dung from the village. Bamboo from the forest. Paper and paint from the Dahanu market.
first_contact: Before festivals I coated the walls with my mother. I still remember the coolness of the dung on my hands.
material_special: The rice white becomes one with the wall. It does not shine, but it stands out in the dim light of our homes.
material_in_hands: Mixed with water, the flour should run evenly down the stick. When it is right, the line walks by itself.
material_spoke: If the paint is too thin it runs. If too thick it sticks to the stick and the line breaks.
correction_action: I add a little water or flour and first draw a line on my fingernail to test. Only then do I touch the wall.
piece_time: Two or three days for a big wall painting, one day on paper. Never rush the chowk.
material_change: Paper and canvas have replaced dung walls.
material_change_reason: Houses became concrete, and paintings must travel outside to be sold.
material_change_gain:
Paper and acrylic took the painting outside. It can be sold, and it doesn't spoil in the rain.

The shine of acrylic feels false. Without the wall, the link with the festival and the home breaks.
occasion_of_use:
The dev chowk at weddings, and on house walls at festivals and harvest.

The smell of wet dung, the Tarpa playing all night, and in the firelight it seems the white people on the wall are dancing.
use_importance: “No chowk, no wedding.” The old women of the village still say this today.
use_feelings: Drawing the chowk I feel devotion and responsibility.
special_vs_everyday: Everyday painting means farming and dance, and it can be sold. The wedding chowk is only for that house.
special_object_rule: Only a suvasini draws the chowk, and songs are sung as it is drawn. The image of Palghat Devi stays there.
special_missing: Without the chowk the wedding feels incomplete; there is no place for the goddess.
not_for_sale_example: The wedding dev chowk and Palghat Devi.
why_protected: She is a goddess, not decoration. We do not accept putting her on a canvas and hanging her on a wall.
safer_alternative: Paintings of the Tarpa dance, farming, forest and festivals. Photos and stories of these can be given.
pride_source: Behind each of my paintings is a true story. That makes me proud.
pride_moment: At an exhibition in Mumbai, a girl stood in the Tarpa circle in front of my painting and began to dance.
recognition_by_others: The knowledgeable women of the village called me to draw the wedding chowk. That is greater than any outside prize.
loss_if_stopped: Our language for telling our stories, our god, and our bond with the land would be gone.
loss_picture: Empty walls, and our story on other people's mugs with no name.
key_stakeholder_of_loss: Our next generation, who would have to read about their own identity in someone else's book.
craft_hours: Four or five hours a day, after farm work. Before festivals we coat and paint walls all day.
change_in_lifetime: Earlier nobody thought of selling a painting. Now children earn from it, but there is competition from printed ‘Warli’ mugs.
artisan_initiated_change: I started a Saturday class for village girls, and began attaching a story card to each painting.
desired_keep:
The rice white, the circular layout, and the rules of the chowk.

Prices set by the middleman, and painting in large numbers at low prices.
strength_anchor: I can tell the story of every painting, and my line moves without stopping. I can teach the girls.
concern_anchor: Our painting is printed on mugs, T-shirts and walls, with no name given and not a rupee paid.
shareable_content:
Tarpa, farming and forest paintings, my name, and details of my class.

The wedding chowk, Palghat Devi, the chowk songs and details of the land dispute.
desired_change:
Companies using Warli should name the artist, and the village should be paid for it.

The chowk will not be sold. It will stay in the village, in the hands of the suvasinis.
learning_story: I painted a hundred identical pictures for a shopkeeper. After the fiftieth, the people had no work left, only lines. I remembered my grandmother's question. Since then I paint only a set number a day.
emotional_story: After my grandmother died, her house wall collapsed in the rain, with the chowk on it. The next year we coated a new wall using that same earth.
clarification_story:
A woman said, what is there to this, just triangles. I gave her the stick and asked her to draw the Tarpa circle. She saw at once that one wrong line breaks the circle.

People think Warli is an easy design. It is our prayer and our history.
